newsitem.title: UK: British group announces gene therapy breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: British group announces gene therapy breakthrough.

text.p: British researchers said on Tuesday they had made a big breakthrough in gene therapy by learning how to deliver toxic drugs to the most impenetrable parts of a tumour.
Adrian Harris of the Institute of Molecular Medicine at Oxford's John Radcliffe hospital and colleagues said they had figured out how to turn a tumour's oxygen-poor environment against it.

"The strategy...is designed to take advantage of the abnormal physiology that exists in almost all solid tumours, regardless of their origin or location," they wrote in a report in the journal Nature Medicine.
Tumours often lack blood supply because they grow so fast. This in turn means less oxygen -- but the tumour cells manage to stay alive and often resist both drugs and radiation therapy.

The researchers -- working with the Medical Research Council and Imperial Cancer Research Fund charities as well as gene therapy specialists Oxford BioMedica Plc -- found out that some genes have a "switch" that turns them on in such oxygen-low or hypoxic conditions.
They spliced this genetic switch -- which they named hypoxia-responsive element (HRE) -- into a modified virus and introduced it into tumour cells first in a test-tube and then in mice.

The idea behind such gene therapy is to use a "vector" such as a weakened virus to deliver a new gene into cells. Viruses are designed to inject their genes into a cell and the hope is they will also inject the therapeutic genes, which will correct whatever genetic defect causes a disease such as cancer.

Harris's HRE approach adds an additional element -- the switch that helps the therapeutic gene work in the oxygen-poor environment. It worked, and they said they were now ready to test the technique in people.

"We are moving quite rapidly towards a clinical trial," said Dr Sue Kingsman, research director at Oxford BioMedica. "We are confident that we are going to be able to include an interesting therapeutic gene," she added in a telephone interview, although she declined to say what gene this might be.

The company, formed in 1995 to develop and commercialise gene therapy technologies, said they could help make cancer treatment easier on the patients, who are often ill and lose hair as a result of drugs or radiation therapy.
"People are always trying to find a way of beating cancer cells without giving the rest of the body a good hiding as well," Kingsman said.
Oxford Biomedica bought the HRE technology from Isis Innovation Ltd, Oxford University's intellectual property company, in February.
The company said in a statement that Phase I and II trials for safety and efficacy in women with breast cancer would start in 1998.

Volunteers will have the engineered genes injected directly into their tumours in the hope that a few will "take" and start turning out proteins that will allow the body's immune system to destroy the tumour cells.
